section_summary: This section documents Allied efforts in late 1941 to prevent Japan from obtaining mercury, cotton, petroleum, metals, ores, and other strategic materials from Latin America, Southeast Asia, and the United States. It includes reports on Mexican mercury smuggling, intergovernmental coordination of export controls, British and Dutch trade restrictions, and Japanese attempts to procure commodities through intermediaries or transshipment points. Cross-reference cards, intelligence reports, correspondence, telegrams, press clippings, and duplicated circulation copies illustrate the State Department’s information-sharing and economic-warfare procedures immediately before and after the United States entered the war.

subfiles.title: Embassy despatch on contraband mercury and metal shipments in Mexico
subfiles.from: Raleigh A. Gibson, for the Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, U.S. Embassy in Mexico
subfiles.about: Reports the contents, routing, financing, and suspected participants in concealed shipments of mercury and other metals in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Continuation: concealed mercury, copper, zinc, antimony, lead and bronze shipments with values; a car from Manzanillo to Tampico was opened under court order; Phillips, Nagabuchi and Mitsubishi funds investigated; President Avila Camacho ordered an inquiry, though the Embassy doubts honest reporting.

subfiles.title: Telegram 639 on preventing Mexican cotton exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports Mexico’s agreement to block a cotton shipment to Japan and its request for help finding a U.S. market.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 639: Mexico's foreign minister says the cotton won't go to Japan but sellers acting in good faith should be protected; Bank of Mexico's Villasenor promises likewise and asks help finding a market.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Mexico concerning a possible U.S. market for cotton
subfiles.from: Cordell Hull, U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: Explains why Mexican cotton withheld from Japan cannot readily be absorbed by the United States.
subfiles.summary: Instruction to thank Mexico for blocking the shipment, noting its U.S. cotton import quota is exhausted and a record American carryover makes an increase impracticable.

subfiles.title: Ross note returning the Mexican cotton case to Collado
subfiles.about: Returns the cotton case for reconsideration after the outbreak of the Pacific war.
subfiles.summary: Ross notes developments presumably ended Peru's cotton shipments to Japan, but recommends returning the Mexican cotton case to Collado.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on inconsistencies in hemispheric cotton export controls
subfiles.about: Compares Mexican cooperation in stopping cotton exports with continued Peruvian sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hawkins notes Mexico stopped a 10,000-20,000-bale shipment while Peru exported 54,776 bales to Japan from August 1 to November 20, raising consistency questions; since the U.S. can't absorb Mexican cotton, he suggests other economic assistance.

subfiles.title: War Department transmittal of intelligence materials
subfiles.from: Sherman Miles, War Department General Staff
subfiles.to: A. A. Berle Jr., Department of State
subfiles.about: Forwards intelligence communications concerning Korean groups, Japanese-American organizations, mercury, and political propaganda.
subfiles.summary: General Sherman Miles forwards intelligence on Syngman Rhee, Japanese organizations, a mercury clipping and propaganda on Roosevelt's ancestry for State's information.

subfiles.title: “Mercury Due To Go To Japs Shows Increase”
subfiles.about: Reports that concealed mercury seized at Manzanillo was more extensive than first estimated.
subfiles.summary: Clipping: Mexican authorities found 1,117 mercury flasks in 162 drums labeled bronze scrap; Attorney General Aguilar y Maya expects the seizure to grow, tied to a U.S.-Mexican economic-defense agreement.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Japanese credits for Peruvian wool and vanadium
subfiles.about: Points to a despatch concerning Japanese credits for purchases of wool and vanadium in Peru.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Japanese credits for Peruvian wool and vanadium, despatch 2028 in file 894.51/754.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Peruvian fuel-oil sale to Japan
subfiles.about: Points to a letter about the Peruvian government’s sale of reserve fuel oil to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: government sale of Peruvian reserve fuel oil to Japanese buyers, file 823.00/1479.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: bootleg mercury shipments
subfiles.about: Points to War Department communications regarding illicit mercury shipments.
subfiles.summary: The card records the transmission of attached communications about bootleg mercury shipments. The original material was filed under 862.24/530.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: possible Japanese acquisition of Brazilian carbonados
subfiles.about: Points to a telegram warning that Brazilian carbonados might go to Japan unless the United States bought the exportable surplus.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Ambassador Caffery's warning on possible Japanese acquisition of Brazilian carbonados, telegram 1567.

subfiles.title: Telegram 1567 on Brazilian carbonado exports
subfiles.about: Requests an immediate decision on purchasing Brazil’s exportable carbonado surplus.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 1567: the Bank of Brazil treats carbonados as industrial diamonds under its U.S. agreement, but American buyers took little, so Caffery warns Brazil may allow exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Hochschild copper sales to Japanese buyers
subfiles.about: Points to information on Mauricio Hochschild’s copper sales from Tocopilla and Coquimbo to Japanese purchasers.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: British Embassy letter on Hochschild copper sales from two Chilean ports, file 811.20 Defense (M)/3589.

subfiles.title: Dent letter on proposed diesel-oil imports for Japanese interests
subfiles.to: Jacques J. Reinstein, Department of State
subfiles.about: Reports plans by the North American Syndicate to import diesel oil and forwards information on suspicious lubricating-oil shipments.
subfiles.summary: Dent: an A-1 Shanghai source says the North American Syndicate hoped to import a tanker of diesel, perhaps via Cathay Oil; he encloses a memorandum on New Orleans shipments and a suspicious 15,000-barrel Whiting oil shipment.

subfiles.title: British memorandum on the HYBERT lubricating-oil cargo
subfiles.about: Analyzes the destinations and consignees of lubricating-oil cargoes shipped from New Orleans aboard the HYBERT.
subfiles.summary: British memorandum compares the HYBERT's declared lubricating-oil cargoes with reports of actual discharge, raising license violations, examines Sterns, Potter, Carlowitz and others, links 15,000 drums to Whiting oil at New Orleans, and recommends investigating Sterns Inc.

subfiles.title: Reinstein note to Yost on the North American Syndicate
subfiles.about: Connects Dent’s report on diesel oil with an attached Cathay Oil Company letter.
subfiles.summary: Reinstein tells Yost that Dent reported a North American Syndicate attempt to arrange diesel shipments for Japanese interests, and forwards a Cathay Oil letter for return.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: proposals for parallel action under the freezing order
subfiles.about: Points to proposals for parallel U.S. action on commodities affected by the freezing order against Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: letter with proposals for parallel action on commodities under the freezing order, Treasury file 840/51 Frozen Credits/3912.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Japanese request for oil-tank storage at Saigon
subfiles.about: Points to a memorandum on Japan’s request to lease oil storage owned by American and British companies at Saigon.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: M. E. Dening's conversation on a Japanese request to lease Standard, Texas and Shell tank storage at Saigon.

subfiles.title: Dent letter on sourcing diesel oil from Mexico or Venezuela
subfiles.to: Jacques J. Reinstein, Department of State
subfiles.about: Reports a North American Syndicate request for as much as 20,000 tons of diesel oil from Mexico or Venezuela.
subfiles.summary: Dent: the North American Syndicate wrote Glenn Smith seeking diesel for electric plants, asking him to look in Mexico or Venezuela, anticipating U.S. disapproval.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Alemán’s comments on Mexican mercury scandals
subfiles.about: Points to a telegram reporting that Miguel Alemán characterized the mercury scandals as ordinary fiscal frauds.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: press reports that Minister Aleman minimized the Mexican mercury cases; telegram 551, file 865.85/636.

subfiles.title: Telegram 551 on Alemán and the mercury scandals
subfiles.about: Reports Alemán’s dismissal of the mercury cases as fiscal fraud and requests authority to question the Mexican Foreign Office.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 551: McGurk says press quoted Miguel Aleman denying any significance beyond fiscal violations; he proposes asking the Foreign Office about it and Mexico's attitude toward German and Italian sailors.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Argentine scrap-rubber shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Points to British information on financing Argentine scrap-rubber exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: a Buenos Aires credit for NAMBEI for scrap rubber; British Singapore rubber licensing must consider Argentine exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Japanese interest in Brazilian strategic minerals
subfiles.about: Points to a warning about Japanese purchases of industrial diamonds, rock crystal, and mica in Brazil.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Brazil urged to keep prohibited strategic materials off the TOA MARU, whose legal cargo is wolfram, cobalt ore and castor oil.

subfiles.title: Telegram 1561 on the TOA MARU and Brazilian exports
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese interest in Brazilian minerals and precautions concerning the TOA MARU.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 1561: Caffery reports Japanese efforts to buy industrial diamonds, rock crystal and mica; he will ask Brazil informally to keep agreement materials off the TOA MARU.

subfiles.title: Marris letter on controlling Thai tin and wolfram sales
subfiles.to: Thomas K. Finletter, Department of State
subfiles.about: Seeks U.S. approval for a commercial organization intended to influence Thai tin and wolfram marketing.
subfiles.summary: Marris: East Asiatic Company proposes, with Yip in Tsoi, to receive southern Thai ores in Malaya and sell by private tender to approved buyers, restoring a friendly presence and possibly allowing later British or American preemption of ore bought for Japan.

subfiles.title: Finletter reply approving the East Asiatic Company proposal
subfiles.about: States that the State Department has no objection to the proposed Thai tin-and-wolfram operation.
subfiles.summary: Finletter acknowledges Marris's East Asiatic Company plan; the Department has no objection.

subfiles.title: British letter on Japanese compensation credits in Peru
subfiles.to: John W. Auchincloss, Department of State
subfiles.about: Reports that Japan would receive Peruvian commodity credits instead of cash compensation for riot damage.
subfiles.summary: After Lima riots Japan claimed about four million soles, reduced by a Peruvian commission to at most one million; compensation will be credits for low-grade wool, salt and sugar, not cash.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japanese attempts to buy Peruvian commodities
subfiles.from: Division of the American Republics, Department of State
subfiles.about: Notes Japanese attempts to acquire Peruvian wool, salt, and sugar amid shipping and exchange constraints.
subfiles.summary: A Lima report says Japanese purchasers sought considerable amounts of the British letter's commodities but got little because of shipping and exchange difficulties; Japan's salt shortage is serious.

subfiles.title: Dent letter on Netherlands East Indies trade controls, first copy
subfiles.to: Jacques J. Reinstein, Department of State
subfiles.about: Describes Netherlands East Indies licensing, blocked-account, commodity-quota, and oil policies toward Japan and China.
subfiles.summary: Dent: the Netherlands East Indies license all exports to Japanese-controlled territories and block Japanese balances; limited nonstrategic goods may be traded for essentials, "nil list" goods are barred, oil stays suspended, and China coast trade is tightly controlled.

subfiles.title: Dent letter on Netherlands East Indies trade controls, second copy
subfiles.to: Jacques J. Reinstein, Department of State
subfiles.about: Circulation copy of the British account of Netherlands East Indies trade restrictions.
subfiles.summary: This duplicate describes licensing for exports to Japan and Japanese-controlled territories, the blocked Japanese account, and annual ceilings for permitted commodities. It repeats the prohibition on goods contributing to Japanese war potential and the conditional suspension of oil shipments.

subfiles.title: Dent letter on Netherlands East Indies trade controls, third copy
subfiles.to: Jacques J. Reinstein, Department of State
subfiles.about: Additional circulation copy of the Netherlands East Indies trade-control report.
subfiles.summary: The third copy again lists commodities allowed in limited quantities and those placed on the strategic “nil list.” It also explains the oil policy and the restrictions governing exports to Japanese and non-Japanese consignees at China coast ports.

subfiles.title: Reinstein acknowledgment of the Netherlands Indies report
subfiles.about: Thanks Dent for supplying detailed information on Netherlands Indies trade with Japan and occupied China.
subfiles.summary: Reinstein acknowledges Dent's November 21 letter; the Department had related information but may lack all the details.

subfiles.title: Embassy despatch on routing Brazilian strategic materials through Chile
subfiles.from: John F. Simmons, for the U.S. Ambassador in Brazil
subfiles.about: Reports evidence that a Japanese firm planned to obtain Brazilian strategic materials through Valparaíso.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy obtained correspondence between an Osaka firm and a Brazilian company describing a plan to ship commodities first to Chile and then transship them to Japan. The materials of current Japanese interest included mineral sand, asbestos, and an OCR-obscured third product, apparently a strategic mineral.

subfiles.title: British letter on stopping Indian cotton exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports that India was being asked to implement its undertaking to reduce cotton shipments to Japan to zero.
subfiles.summary: Hall told London U.S. cotton exports to Japan were zero in August and expected zero in September; London advised India to allow no October shipments except under pre-freezing credits or cash contracts.

subfiles.title: Acheson reply on November cotton-export licenses
subfiles.about: Reports that the Treasury issued no licenses for cotton exports to Japan during November.
subfiles.summary: Acheson answers Hall's October 2 inquiry: Treasury issued no cotton export licenses to Japan in November.

subfiles.title: Acheson letter to Stopford on cotton exports
subfiles.about: Provides figures on the absence of raw-cotton licenses for Japan and shipments to China.
subfiles.summary: Acheson tells Stopford Treasury issued no raw-cotton licenses for Japan in October and apparently none in September, giving September figures for China and a tentative October estimate of 300,537 pounds ($50,045) for occupied China.

subfiles.title: Dent letter clearing a Central American cotton shipment to Shanghai
subfiles.about: Reports that British objections to a Central American cotton shipment from San Francisco were withdrawn after a satisfactory sale.
subfiles.summary: British Consulate General objected to Central American cotton sent forward unsold; after sale to an unobjectionable buyer with assurances, the Embassy told its San Francisco consulate to withdraw the objection.

subfiles.title: Military Intelligence current-events report on Mexico
subfiles.from: Frederick D. Sharp, Military Intelligence Division
subfiles.about: Summarizes Mexican press reporting on agriculture, labor, petroleum, politics, railroads, foreign relations, contraband, and public works.
subfiles.summary: The digest compiles press reports on agricultural imports and exports, telephone assets, banking, labor disputes, petroleum accidents, railway equipment, blacklisting, education, infrastructure, and political affairs. Of particular relevance to this file, it alleges several mercury-smuggling operations to Japan through Manzanillo and Tampico and claims that Socorro Island served as a contraband center. It also notes the arrival of Japanese rayon and other indicators of continuing trade.

subfiles.title: Instruction 4406 requesting information on Mexican mercury smuggling
subfiles.to: Josephus Daniels, U.S. Ambassador to Mexico
subfiles.about: Requests investigation of press allegations about mercury shipments through Manzanillo, Tampico, and Socorro Island.
subfiles.summary: The Department quotes a Military Intelligence press digest alleging one intercepted Manzanillo shipment, an earlier undetected shipment, another seizure at Tampico, and use of Socorro Island as a smuggling base. It asks the Embassy for additional information and for recommendations to improve Mexican enforcement against contraband exports.

subfiles.title: Reinstein acknowledgment of Dent’s cotton-shipment letter
subfiles.about: Thanks Dent for information about the Central American cotton shipment to Shanghai.
subfiles.summary: Reinstein acknowledges Dent's November 25 report on cotton held at San Francisco and thanks the British Embassy.

subfiles.title: Embassy despatch 14407 on contraband shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: Raleigh A. Gibson, for the Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, U.S. Embassy in Mexico
subfiles.about: Answers the Department’s inquiry into alleged mercury smuggling from Mexico to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 14407: the Mexican Navy doubted the Socorro Island story; the alleged 150-drum shipment was Phillips's cargo on the HEIGO MARU, with no evidence of mercury; Gibson blames corrupt port officials and urges rapid consular reporting.

subfiles.title: Consular despatch on a reported mercury shipment to Aguascalientes
subfiles.from: Harold S. Tewell, American Consulate General, Havana
subfiles.about: Forwards a letter excerpt possibly related to a reported mercury seizure in Mexico destined for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Tewell reports indirect word that mercury was seized at Agua Caliente for Japan, and an informant found an excerpt among returned manuscripts, possibly signed by or to Francisco Ortega.

subfiles.title: Excerpt of letter seeking a quotation for 8,000 kilograms of mercury
subfiles.about: Requests a rapid price quotation for mercury delivered to Aguascalientes or the border.
subfiles.summary: Frank mentions contacts with Del Llano and a textile seller, and asks a quick per-kilogram quotation for 8,000 kilograms of mercury in Aguascalientes or at the border.

subfiles.title: State Department transmittal of the Havana mercury report
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division; Office of Naval Intelligence; Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Distributes the Havana consular despatch and its mercury-related enclosure to U.S. intelligence agencies.
subfiles.summary: State transmits Havana despatch 3182 on mercury and its enclosure for use by military, naval and federal investigators.

subfiles.title: Embassy despatch 14485 on Mexican cotton intended for Japan
subfiles.from: J. F. McGurk, U.S. Embassy in Mexico
subfiles.about: Requests an early response to Mexico’s proposal that the United States find a market for cotton withheld from Japan.
subfiles.summary: McGurk reviews the proposed 10,000-20,000-bale Mexican cotton shipment; Foreign Minister Padilla again asks whether Washington has replied on a U.S. market, and McGurk requests prompt instructions.

subfiles.title: Memorandum against further mercury-control representations to Mexico
subfiles.about: Argues that further U.S. suggestions on stopping Mexican mercury exports would be diplomatically inappropriate after the break with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Memo argues against more mercury-control representations: Mexico had severed relations with Japan, so further measures against shipments to a virtual enemy were unnecessary and indelicate.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: proposed magnesium-for-bauxite exchange
subfiles.from: State Department, Division of Trade Agreements (Bunn)
subfiles.about: Points to a memorandum on a proposed exchange of Japanese magnesium for British bauxite.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: British Embassy official Therold's views on a proposed magnesium-for-bauxite exchange, file 811.20 Defense (M)/3873.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: alleged Japanese oil from the United States
subfiles.about: Points to a letter and clippings from Thomas Fish concerning Japanese acquisition of U.S. oil.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Ready Tool Company letter with clippings alleging Japan obtains oil from the United States.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: strategic-material shipments from Antofagasta
subfiles.about: Points to reports on strategic materials shipped from the Antofagasta district to Japan in August 1941.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: reports on Japanese-bound strategic materials from northern Chile, file 811.20 Defense (M) Chile/51.

subfiles.title: Naval intelligence paraphrase on a suspicious steamer off the Suchiate River
subfiles.about: Reports an unidentified vessel possibly connected with southbound Mexican mercury smuggling.
subfiles.summary: Naval intelligence: an unidentified steamer lay off the Suchiate River on October 30 and sailed south, possibly linked to rumors of Mexican mercury moved south for Japanese ships.

subfiles.title: Instruction 4390 forwarding the Suchiate River report
subfiles.about: Confidentially forwards the government report of a suspicious steamer near the Suchiate River.
subfiles.summary: Instruction 4390 quotes the November 5 report on possible Mexican mercury smuggling and gives it to the Ambassador in strict confidence for investigation.

subfiles.title: Anonymous handwritten letter urging a complete break with Japan
subfiles.about: Urges Roosevelt to cut off trade with Japan and alleges that Pauline Gerli had Japanese and Italian connections.
subfiles.summary: The writer praises firm action against Japanese imports and exports and urges the United States to sever ties completely. The letter claims inside knowledge that silk importer Pauline Gerli was close to Mitsui, Mitsubishi, Galeazzo Ciano, and Benito Mussolini and held substantial assets in Japan under an assumed Japanese identity.

subfiles.title: State Department transmittal of the anonymous Gerli allegation
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division; Office of Naval Intelligence; Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Distributes an anonymous letter concerning Pauline Gerli’s alleged Japanese and Italian connections.
subfiles.summary: State forwards the anonymous Gerli allegation to three federal intelligence agencies as possibly useful, leaving evaluation to them.

subfiles.title: Typed copy of anonymous letter to President Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Reproduces the anonymous appeal for a total trade cutoff against Japan and allegations about Pauline Gerli.
subfiles.summary: Typed anonymous letter to Roosevelt urges cutting off Japan entirely before negotiating, and claims Pauline Gerli was tied to Mitsui, Mitsubishi, Ciano and Mussolini and kept over a million dollars in Japan under a Japanese name.

subfiles.title: Acheson memorandum of conversation with Noel Hall
subfiles.about: Records confidential discussions of U.S. petroleum, cotton, and iron-ore controls affecting Japan.
subfiles.summary: Acheson tells Noel Hall freezing controls have stopped U.S. petroleum exports to Japan, with prior consultation if policy changes; they discuss tying Indian cotton limits to U.S. exports and coordinating Malayan iron-ore policy with Philippine quotas, with the oil assurance tightly held.

subfiles.title: Fragmentary note on a reported petrol sale to Japan
subfiles.about: Records a fragmentary allegation that 200 tons of petrol had been sold to Japanese buyers.
subfiles.summary: Fragmentary note: someone sold 200 tons of petrol to "the Japs"; a second fragment mentions a minister and Germany; identities illegible.

subfiles.title: Reinstein memorandum to Fisher on blocked nationals
subfiles.about: Recommends holding a British inquiry pending guidance on dealings with blocked nationals in Latin America.
subfiles.summary: Reinstein thinks the British raised blocked nationals informally on purpose; at Hiss's suggestion he proposes awaiting a circular on applying Executive Order 8389 to Americans in Latin America dealing with blocked nationals not on the Proclaimed List.

subfiles.title: Dent letter on Argentine cotton sales to Japan
subfiles.about: Seeks U.S. views on discouraging a proposed Argentine cotton sale to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Dent: Bunge & Born asked the British Embassy in Buenos Aires about selling 200-300 tons of Argentine cotton on a Japanese steamer; he asks whether Washington agrees the Embassy should discourage such sales.

subfiles.title: Hall letter requesting final cotton-export figures
subfiles.about: Acknowledges information on cotton licenses and asks to receive final figures for exports to China.
subfiles.summary: Hall says London was told Treasury granted no raw-cotton licenses for Japan in October, and asks Acheson for final China export figures when available.

subfiles.title: British Embassy compliments slip forwarding a copy to Herbert Feis
subfiles.about: Forwards Feis a copy of a letter sent that day to Jacques Reinstein.
subfiles.summary: British Embassy compliments slip forwarding to Herbert Feis a copy of a November 17 letter to Reinstein.

subfiles.title: Copy of British letter concerning Mexican dealings and the Proclaimed List
subfiles.about: Reports additional information concerning Mexican activity and a person or entity on the U.S. Proclaimed List.
subfiles.summary: Badly degraded copy of a British letter: further information from similar sources concerns the Mexican government and the Proclaimed List; names illegible.
